Subject to dynamic instability (transitions between growth and catastrophe) regulated by GTP hydrolysis. Originate from the centrosome (MTOC) via the γ-TuRC complex.Kinesins (anterograde transport toward + end) and Cytoplasmic Dyneins (retrograde transport toward – end) coupled to the dynactin complex.Organelle and vesicular trafficking, chromosome segregation via the mitotic spindle, motile architecture, and ciliary/flagellar beating (9+2 axonemal structure mediated by axonemal dynein).

ENDOMEMBRANE TRAFFICKING FLOW

The endomembrane system forms a dynamic interconnected network via budding transport vesicles coated by specific protein coats (COPI, COPII, Clathrin). Membrane targeting and fusion selectivity are ensured by small GTPases of the Rab family and SNARE receptor complexes (v-SNARE on vesicle, t-SNARE on target membrane):

1. Biosynthesis & Folding (RER)
Translocation and Quality Control
Signal peptide recognition via SRP, co-translational translocation through the Sec61 channel into the RER lumen. Co-translational N-glycosylation (oligosaccharide transfer of Glc3Man9GlcNAc2) and chaperone-mediated folding control (Calnexin/Calreticulin, BiP). Misfolded protein elimination via ERAD (Endoplasmic-Reticulum-Associated Degradation). COPII-coated vesicles for anterograde transport to the Golgi.
↓
2. Processing & Sorting (Golgi)
Maturation and Selective Targeting
Sequential transit through cis, medial, and trans-Golgi compartments. Oligosaccharide chain modification (mannose trimming, O-glycosylation on Ser/Thr residues, sulfation, and phosphorylation). Terminal sorting toward cellular destinations in the trans-Golgi Network (TGN). COPI vesicles regulate retrograde traffic back to the RER (retrieval of C-terminal KDEL sequence).
↓
3a. Secretory Pathway / Exocytosis
Membrane & External Secretion
Constitutive release (membrane lipoprotein renewal) or regulated release (storage in secretory granules released upon extracellular Ca2+ stimulation, e.g., hormones, neurotransmitters) via fusion driven by the v/t-SNARE complex.
3b. Endo-Lysosomal Pathway
Lytic & Autophagic Compartment
Recognition of hydrolases tagged with Mannose-6-Phosphate (M6P) by the MPR receptor in the TGN. Budding of Clathrin-coated vesicles with AP-1 adaptor, destined for fusion with late endosomes and lysosomes.

CELLULAR ORGANELLES: BIOENERGETICS AND HOMEOSTASIS

Metabolic coordination relies on the compartmentalization of specialized reactions within highly evolved subcellular organelles:

  • Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum (SER): Tubular network devoid of ribosomes. Governs structural lipid biosynthesis (phospholipids, cholesterol) and steroid hormones, glycogen metabolism (via glucose-6-phosphatase), and xenobiotic/apolar drug detoxification driven by Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases. In muscle cells, it forms the sarcoplasmic reticulum, specialized in rapid Ca2+ sequestration and release via SERCA pumps and ryanodine receptors (RyR).
  • Mitochondria and Bioenergetics: Semiautonomous endosymbiotic organelles bounded by a double membrane (outer membrane permeable via porins, inner membrane folded into cristae with high electrical resistance, rich in cardiolipin). The matrix lumen contains its own circular genome (mtDNA) and 55S mitoribosomes. Site of pyruvate oxidative decarboxylation, fatty acid β-oxidation, and the Krebs cycle. Inner membrane respiratory complexes (I, II, III, IV) transfer electrons to molecular oxygen (O2), pumping protons into the intermembrane space to generate proton-motive force (Δp):

    Δp = ΔΨm − (2.303 · R · T / F) · ΔpH

    where ΔΨm represents the mitochondrial membrane electrical potential (≈ −160 / −180 mV) and ΔpH ≈ 0.5–1.0 pH units. Inward proton flow into the matrix powers the rotational motor of FoF1-ATP Synthase for ADP phosphorylation:

    ADP + Pi + 4 H+intermembrane → ATP + H2O + 4 H+matrix
  • Lysosomes and Peroxisomes: Lysosomes are single-bilayer catabolic vesicles containing acid hydrolases (pH ≈ 4.5–5.0 maintained by active proton pumping via v-ATPase); they play key roles in heterophagy, organellar autophagy (macroautophagy), and crinophagy. Peroxisomes are oxidative organelles utilizing flavoprotein oxidases to produce hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), scavenged by catalase:

    2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2

    They also perform α- and β-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs, C ≥ 22).
  • Cell Nucleus, Nuclear Envelope, and Chromatin: Repository of the genome, separated from the cytosol by a double bilayer interrupted by Nuclear Pore Complexes (NPCs, composed of nucleoporins) regulating Ran GTPase-guided nuclear-cytoplasmic traffic (RanGAP/RanGEF). Contains the nucleolus and chromatin: euchromatin (decondensed, actively transcribed, enriched in H3K9ac and H3K4me3) and heterochromatin (hypercondensed, silenced, categorized as constitutive or facultative and marked by H3K9me3 and H3K27me3).
en.dna_structure_section:
DNA: MOLECULAR ARCHITECTURE AND GENETIC INFORMATION STORAGE

Executive Summary: Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is a polyanionic informational biopolymer whose fundamental monomeric unit is the NUCLEOTIDE. In its thermodynamically favored physiological conformation in aqueous solution (B-DNA), the macromolecule structures into a right-handed double helix composed of two antiparallel polynucleotide chains (with stereospecific 5'→3' and 3'→5' orientation) wound around a common central axis.

Each nucleotide monomer is articulated into three biochemically distinct domains:

  • Hydrophilic Outer Scaffold (Polyanionic Backbone):
    • Phosphate group esterified at C-5' of the sugar (fully ionized at physiological pH, imparting an equivalent net negative charge and a strong surface electrostatic potential)
    • Furanose pentose (2'-deoxy-D-ribose), with C2'-endo sugar pucker conformation typical of B-DNA
  • Hydrophobic Inner Core and Heterocyclic Bases:
    • Heterocyclic nitrogenous bases linked via β-N-glycosidic bond at C-1' in anti conformation: Bicyclic Purines [Adenine (A), Guanine (G)] and Monocyclic Pyrimidines [Cytosine (C), Thymine (T)]

Single-strand polymerization occurs via covalent phosphodiester bonds between the alpha phosphate group linked to C-5' of one deoxyribose and the nucleophilic hydroxyl (-OH) group at the 3' position of the adjacent sugar. The assembly and thermodynamic stability of the complementary duplex are driven by specific Watson-Crick hydrogen bonds directed toward the duplex core — 2 H-bonds for the A=T pair and 3 H-bonds for the G≡C pair —, combined with the dominant contribution of hydrophobic base stacking mediated by van der Waals interactions and π-orbital overlap between adjacent heterocyclic rings (helical pitch of 3.4 nm for 10.5 base pairs per turn, featuring major and minor grooves).

The primary nucleotide sequence constitutes the master coding sequence of the cell, wherein the outer phosphodiester backbone provides chemical protection and hydrolytic stability to the central core. Genetic information, decoded in non-overlapping triplets (codons) via a degenerate and nearly universal GENETIC CODE, finely determines the transcriptome and proteomic profile, governing molecular dynamics, homeostasis, and the phenotypic properties of the entire organism.
en.genes_proteins_chromosomes_section:
GENES, PROTEINS AND CHROMOSOMES: GENOME PRESERVATION AND EXPRESSION

Executive Summary: The genomic DNA stores coding information, coordinating vital functions through genes — nucleotide sequences that direct the synthesis of RNA and proteins. The directional flow of molecular information proceeds from DNA to RNA to proteins. In eukaryotes, the entire genome (approximately 2 meters of linear DNA per nucleus) undergoes massive, organized condensation with histone proteins to structure into 46 chromosomes (Diploid set 2n = 46), divided into autosomes and sex chromosomes inherited parentally.

GENES AS FUNDAMENTAL INFORMATIONAL UNITS AND CISTRON ARCHITECTURE

The nuclear and mitochondrial genome governs cellular homeostasis by regulating the spatiotemporal transcription of informational sequences. A GENE is defined as a continuous or discontinuous polynucleotide segment (interspersed with exons and introns in eukaryotes) equipped with regulatory regions (promoters, enhancers, silencers) that codes for a functional RNA transcript: messenger RNA (mRNA), transfer RNA (tRNA), ribosomal RNA (rRNA), or regulatory ncRNAs (miRNA, lncRNA). Through the translational machinery, mRNA is converted into a polypeptide chain with a specific primary structure. Derived proteins — catalytic enzymes, cytoskeletal elements, transducer receptors, and transcription factors — determine the METABOLIC KINETICS, PROLIFERATION, AND DIFFERENTIATION of the cytotype.

Each species and individual expresses a distinct proteomic profile (dynamic proteome), resulting from post-transcriptional processing (alternative splicing) and post-translational modifications (phosphorylation, glycosylation, ubiquitination), ultimately establishing the molecular phenotype and penetrance of hereditary traits.

THE CENTRAL DOGMA OF MOLECULAR BIOLOGY AND INFORMATIONAL FLOW

The central dogma describes the directional transfer of genetic information between sequential biopolymers, articulated through the primary processes of transcription and translation:

Phase 1 · Nuclear Compartment
TRANSCRIPTION
pre-mRNA / mRNA Synthesis
The enzyme RNA Polymerase II catalyzes the synthesis of an RNA strand complementary to the template strand of DNA (3'→5'), followed by 5'-capping, polyadenylation, and splicing.
Phase 2 · Cytosolic Compartment
TRANSLATION
Ribosomal Polypeptide Synthesis
80S ribosomes and aminoacylated tRNAs decode the nucleotide codon sequence on mRNA according to the rules of the genetic code.
↓
Functional Outcome / Phenotype
DNA → RNA → FUNCTIONAL PROTEIN
Three-dimensional folding of the amino acid chain (self-assembling folding) and maturation into the final effector protein to modulate the metabolic and signal transduction network.

CHROMOSOMES, HISTONE CONDENSATION AND CHROMATIN ORGANIZATION

CHROMOSOMES represent the highest supramolecular condensation state of chromatin, visually observable during mitotic or meiotic metaphase. In this phase, the duplicated chromosome is structured into two identical SISTER CHROMATIDS, held together by cohesin protein complexes and joined at the primary constricted region termed the CENTROMERE, which serves as the assembly site for the macromolecular kinetochore complex to anchor spindle microtubules.

The structural framework of chromosomes relies on chromatin, a nucleoprotein complex formed by the association of DNA with highly positively charged basic proteins (HISTONES H2A, H2B, H3, H4 forming the octameric nucleosome core, and linker HISTONE H1) alongside regulatory non-histone proteins. This superstructure scales from "beads-on-a-string" nucleosomes (11 nm) up to topologically associating domains (TADs) and higher-order structures for genomic segregation and hereditary transmission.

HUMAN KARYOTYPE, CYTOGENETICS AND GAMETIC PLOIDY

The nucleus of every human somatic cell harbors a linear genome roughly 2 meters long, organized into the diploid karyotype consisting of 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 homologous pairs. Each homologous pair shares matching synteny, morphology, and gene loci occupied by equivalent or alternative alleles, derived from paternal and maternal origin respectively.

The first 22 pairs consist of morpho-functionally overlapping non-sex chromosomes termed AUTOSOMES (numbered 1 through 22 based on cytogenetic size); the 23rd pair comprises the HETEROCROMOSOMES or SEX CHROMOSOMES (GONOSOMES), which establish biological sex and sex-linked inheritance patterns:

  • Biological male: heterogametic and heteromorphic set 46,XY
  • Biological female: homogametic and homomorphic set 46,XX

In sexual reproduction dynamics, meiosis reduces the chromosome complement: mature germ cells or gametes (sperm and oocytes) acquire a reduced set of 23 single-chromatid chromosomes, establishing a haploid (n) state. Upon syngamy (fertilization), the fusion of the two gametic pronuclei restores the diploid condition (2n = 46) in the zygote, ensuring recombinational variability and maintaining species-specific chromosome counts in somatic cells.
en.cell_division_section:
CELL DIVISION: MITOSIS, MEIOSIS AND REPRODUCTION

Executive Summary: Cellular proliferation occurs through two fundamental processes tightly regulated by CDK-cyclin complexes: mitosis, a highly faithful equational division generating two clone-identical diploid daughter cells for homeostasis and tissue regeneration, and meiosis, a reductional division characteristic of the germline that reduces ploidy from diploid to haploid to generate recombined gametes via crossing-over. Subsequent syngamy (fertilization) restores diploidy in the totipotent zygote.

MITOSIS AND SOMATIC CELL PROLIFERATION

Somatic cell proliferation occurs through mitotical equational division: the progenitor cell segregates its macromolecular content via MITOSIS, coordinated by MPF complex (CDK1/Cyclin B) activation and monitored by the Spindle Assembly Checkpoint (SAC).

This division cycle ensures faithful and karyotypically invariant transmission of DNA to both daughter cells. This accuracy relies on high-fidelity S-phase semiconservative replication and the biomechanical interaction of kinetochore microtubules with centromeres at the metaphase plate, followed by proteasomal degradation of securin and separase-mediated cohesin cleavage during anaphase. Subsequent cytokinesis is driven by the constriction of an actin-myosin II contractile ring regulated by RhoA GTPase, evenly partitioning the cytosol and organelle network.

Although mitosis occurs in somatic cells capable of passing the restriction point (G0/G1), replicative capacity varies radically: from terminally differentiated perennial cytotypes to unspecialized pools known as stem cells. These maintain self-renewal potential through asymmetric division, preserving the niche while giving rise to transit-amplifying cells destined for differentiation across tissue compartments.

MEIOSIS AND GENERATION OF GENETIC VARIABILITY

The meiotic germline follows an exclusive cleavage pathway of sexual cells (primary gametocytes) committed to gametogenesis (spermatogenesis and oogenesis): MEIOSIS.

Biologically, the meiotic cycle consists of two consecutive nuclear and cellular divisions (reductional Meiosis I and equational Meiosis II) preceded by a single DNA replication phase. This cycle converts a diploid germ cell (2n) into functional units with a haploid (n) genomic complement.

Meiosis culminates in the formation of four haploid daughter cells, possessing unique and recombined genetic profiles. During prolonged prophase I (subdivided into leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, and diakinesis), homologous chromosomes pair to form tetrads stabilized by the synaptonemal complex. During this stage, crossing-over (homologous recombination) occurs, catalyzed by recombinative endonucleases (e.g., SPO11) through double-strand breaks and physical exchange of non-sister DNA segments (visible as chiasmata). This event, coupled with random orientation and independent assortment of homologous pairs at metaphase I, constitutes the molecular engine of phylogenetic evolution and intraspecific phenotypic diversity.

SEXUAL REPRODUCTION AND SYNGAMY

Meiosis serves as the obligatory preparatory maturation event for sexual reproduction (amphimixis); gametic fusion and allelic recombination increase heterozygosity and purge deleterious mutations from the population gene pool.

Each gamete contributes a single-chromatid haploid chromosome set (n): the maternal secondary oocyte (arrested at metaphase II until sperm contact) and the paternal flagellated spermatozoon. The process of fertilization (syngamy) initiates with receptor binding to the zona pellucida (ZP3), triggering the acrosome reaction as well as rapid (membrane depolarization) and slow (cortical reaction and Ca2+-dependent granule exocytosis) blocks to polyspermy. Fusion of the two cell membranes and subsequent karyogamy of the pronuclei restores the diploid state (2n = 46) in the totipotent zygote, initiating early cleavage divisions of embryonic development.
en.organelles_structures_section:
CELLULAR ORGANELLES: STRUCTURE, BIOENERGETICS AND COMPARTMENTAL HOMEOSTASIS

In summary: Cellular compartmentalization is structured along three primary physiological axes:

  • Gene and Energy Flow: Nucleus and Mitochondria (double-membrane organelles) preside over genome preservation and transcription, and ATP synthesis via electrochemical proton gradient and chemiosmotic coupling.
  • Biosynthesis and Vesicular Traffic: Endoplasmic Reticulum and Golgi Apparatus coordinate co-translational translocation, chaperone-guided folding, post-translational modifications (glycosylation), and targeted sorting via coated vesicles (COPI, COPII, Clathrin), while managing Ca2+ sequestration.
  • Oxidation, Lytic Clearance, and Redox: Peroxisomes and Lysosomes regulate very long-chain fatty acid (VLCFA) beta-oxidation, catalase-mediated reactive oxygen species (ROS) neutralization, and autophagic and heterophagic catabolic flows coordinated by high acidic proton gradient hydrolases.

1. DOUBLE-MEMBRANE COMPARTMENTS: GENE FLOW AND BIOENERGETICS

CELL NUCLEUS AND NUCLEAR PORE COMPLEX (NPC)
Primary site of the nuclear genome, enclosed by a double phospholipid bilayer nuclear envelope with a perinuclear lumen structurally continuous with the RER. Nucleocytoplasmic communication is regulated by Nuclear Pore Complexes (NPCs), macromolecular structures exceeding 110 MDa composed of over 30 distinct nucleoporins (NUPs). Selective transport of hydrophilic macromolecules larger than 40 kDa is strictly dependent on transport receptors (Karyopherins: Importins and Exportins) and driven by the gradient slope of the monomeric GTPase Ran, maintained in the Ran-GTP state in the nucleus (via the exchange factor RCC1) and Ran-GDP in the cytosol (via RanGAP).

MITOCHONDRION: BIOENERGETICS AND CHEMIOSMOTIC COUPLING
Semiautonomous endosymbiotic organelle equipped with circular DNA (mtDNA) and bacterial-like ribosomes (70S). The inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM), highly impermeable and rich in cardiolipin, invaginates into cristae housing the electron transport chain (ETC, Complexes I-IV). Oxidation of reduced coenzymes (NADH and FADH2) generates a transmembrane electrochemical potential (Δp composed of ΔΨ of approximately -180 mV and a pH gradient of about 0.75 units). This gradient forces protons back into the matrix through the Fo channel of FoF1-ATP Synthase, driving gamma stalk rotation and ATP synthesis from ADP and Pi. The mitochondrion also presides over the Krebs cycle, fatty acid beta-oxidation, and, under oxidative stress or Ca2+ overload, the triggering of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway via mPTP pore opening and release of cytochrome c into the cytosol.

2. ENDOMEMBRANE SYSTEM: BIOSYNTHESIS, HOMEOSTASIS AND VESICULAR TRAFFIC

ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM (E.R.)
Three-dimensional network of cisternae and tubules dedicated to biosynthesis and ionic balance, divided into domains:

  • Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (R.E.R.): Associated with ribosomes anchored via translocon subunits (Sec61). Presides over co-translational translocation guided by signal recognition particles (SRP) and folding assisted by molecular chaperones (BiP/GRP78, Calnexin, Calreticulin) and protein disulfide isomerase (PDI). Site of N-glycosylation initiation on Asparagine residues (Asn-X-Ser/Thr).
  • Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum (S.E.R.): Tubular organization lacking ribosomal elements. Central site for membrane phospholipid, cholesterol, and steroid hormone synthesis. Serves as the primary intracellular reservoir for Ca2+ ions via active SERCA ATPase pump action. In hepatic tissues, expresses high levels of Cytochrome P450 (CYP450) superfamily isoenzymes dedicated to lipophilic xenobiotic and drug detoxification.

GOLGI APPARATUS AND VESICULAR TRAFFIC DYNAMICS
Polarized stack of cisternae structurally divided into cis-Golgi Network (CGN), Medial Golgi, and trans-Golgi Network (TGN). Receives vesicles from the RER shaped by COPII coat protein (anterograde transport), while recycling resident RER proteins bearing the KDEL sequence via COPI vesicles (retrograde transport). Subsequent glycan maturation and O-glycosylation on Serine/Threonine residues occur within the cisternae. In the TGN, biomolecules are packaged into Clathrin-coated vesicles or other adaptor proteins, targeting them selectively to the plasma membrane or endo-lysosomal compartment via Mannose-6-Phosphate (M6P) tagging.

3. METABOLIC COMPARTMENTS AND LYTIC CLEARANCE

PEROXISOME: OXIDATIVE METABOLISM AND REDOX HOMEOSTASIS
Single-membrane organelle importing matrix proteins via targeting sequences (PTS1 or PTS2) recognized by peroxins (PEX). Primary compartment for very long-chain fatty acid (from C22 upwards, VLCFA) and branched-chain fatty acid beta-oxidation, catalyzed by acyl-CoA oxidase producing hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). The tetrameric catalase enzyme instantly decomposes H2O2 into H2O and O2, preventing oxidative stress. Also plays key roles in plasmalogen biosynthesis.

LYSOSOME: MACROMOLECULAR DEGRADATION AND AUTOPHAGY
Single-membrane vesicle containing over 60 acid hydrolases (proteases, nucleases, lipases, glycosidases) characterized by optimal activity at pH between 4.5 and 5.0. The internal proton gradient is generated by active pumping of V-type H+-ATPase consuming ATP. The lysosomal membrane is protected from self-digestion by a dense coat of highly glycosylated glycoproteins (LAMP-1, LAMP-2). The lysosomal compartment serves as the convergence point for three main pathways:

  • Autophagy (Macroautophagy): Sequestration of cytosol portions or senescent organelles into double-membrane autophagosomes, regulated by the ULK1 complex and coordinated by LC3-II, followed by fusion with the lysosome (autolysosome).
  • Heterophagy and Endocytosis: Fusion with late endosomes containing extracellular material internalized via receptor-mediated endocytosis or pinocytosis.
  • Phagocytosis: Internalization and elimination of large particles, cellular debris, or pathogens by specialized cells forming the phagolysosome.

en.tissues_section:
BIOLOGICAL TISSUES AND TISSUE ORGANIZATION

In summary: Tissues are coordinated sets of specialized cells that cooperate to perform complex biological functions, embedded in a supporting scaffold known as the extracellular matrix. The organism is divided into four fundamental types: epithelial (protective barriers and linings), connective (support, nutrition, and connection), muscle (force generation and movement), and nervous (conduction of electrical impulses). Epithelia, in particular, form compact layers lacking direct vascularization, nourished by diffusion from the underlying connective tissue.

TISSUE ORGANIZATION AND EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX

A tissue constitutes an integrated level of biological organization composed of a consortium of specialized cells sharing embryonic origin, morphological characteristics, and functional cooperation. These cellular populations are structured and coordinated via the extracellular matrix (ECM), a macromolecular network of highly variable chemical composition and consistency.

The four fundamental biological tissues of the human body are classified as:

  • Epithelial Tissue: tightly adjoined cells forming protective, absorptive, or secretory barriers.
  • Connective Tissue (or supportive tissue): prominent extracellular matrix providing structural support, mechanical protection, and metabolic exchange.
  • Muscle Tissue: contractile elements specialized in force generation and movement.
  • Nervous Tissue: excitable cells responsible for receiving, processing, and transmitting bioelectric impulses.

EPITHELIAL TISSUE: POLARITY, JUNCTIONS, AND AVASCULARITY

Epithelial tissue is characterized by tightly bound, structurally polarized cells (apical, lateral, and basal domains), in which the intercellular extracellular matrix is reduced to thin clefts.

Mechanical cohesion and intercellular space sealing are provided by lateral plasma membrane specializations forming the transmembrane junctional complex stabilized by the cytoskeleton (occluding junctions/tight junctions, anchoring junctions/desmosomes, and communicating junctions/gap junctions).

Epithelia are divided into three primary functional categories: covering epithelia (protective, absorptive, or excretory barriers), glandular epithelia (specialized in exocrine or endocrine secretory activity), and sensory epithelia (modified epithelial cells for stimulus reception, e.g., taste buds).

Epithelial tissue consistently rests upon underlying connective tissue, anchored via the intervening basal membrane (an acellular structure rich in type IV collagen, laminin, and proteoglycans). Because epithelial tissue is completely avascular (lacking intrinsic blood vessels), metabolic oxygen and nutrient exchange occurs exclusively by passive diffusion across the basal membrane from connective tissue capillary beds.

HISTOLOGICAL CLASSIFICATION OF COVERING EPITHELIA

Covering epithelia are histologically classified based on surface cell morphology and the number of constituent cell layers:

  • Simple (unilayered) epithelium: composed of a single cell layer resting on the basal membrane; optimized for diffusion, absorption, and filtration processes (e.g., pulmonary alveoli, renal tubules).
  • Stratified (multilayered) epithelium: composed of multiple overlapping cell layers, with only the basal layer contacting the basal membrane; specialized in protection against mechanical and chemical insults (e.g., keratinized epidermis, esophageal mucosa).
  • Pseudostratified epithelium: a unilayered variant where all cells touch the basal membrane but, due to varying heights and staggered nuclear levels, simulate a multilayered arrangement on histological cross-section (e.g., ciliated respiratory epithelium).
en.epithelial_connective_section:
EPITHELIAL FUNCTIONS AND CONNECTIVE TISSUE ARCHITECTURE

In summary: Epithelia form selective lining barriers and specialized glandular parenchyma for exocrine and endocrine secretion. Connective tissue provides trophomechanical support, characterized by an abundant, hydrated extracellular matrix (ECM) reinforced by protein fibers, which specializes into connective tissue proper, cartilage, adipose, and bone tissue.

Functions of Lining Epithelia

They line the outer surface of the body (the epidermis, keratinized epithelial tissue of the skin), channels and hollow organs communicating with the exterior (forming the epithelium of the mucous membrane), the lumens of blood and lymphatic vessels (constituting the endothelium), and internal closed serous cavities and associated organs (constituting the protective mesothelium of pleura, pericardium, and peritoneum).

Cytological differentiation, number of layers, and specific anatomical localization strictly dictate the functional properties of the epithelium (mechanical protection, selective absorption, secretion, chemical-physical barrier, or molecular transport).

Glandular Epithelia

Glandular epithelia consist of cells specialized in anabolism and regulated secretion of biologically active substances, termed secretions. These cells can operate as isolated unicellular secretory elements or organize into complex parenchyma forming glands.

Glands are subdivided and classified primarily based on their mode, morphology, and pathway of secretion release. Based on the topography of release, they are distinguished into:

  • Exocrine glands: secrete products onto the external body surface or into the lumen of a hollow organ via excretory ducts lined by epithelial cells.
  • Endocrine glands: lacking excretory ducts, release chemical messengers called hormones directly into the interstitial space to diffuse into the bloodstream toward distant target organs.

Connective Tissue

Connective tissue is histologically characterized by a volumetric predominance of extracellular matrix over the cellular component. The ECM consists of an amorphous ground substance (a hydrogel rich in water, glycosaminoglycans, proteoglycans, and structural glycoproteins) embedding cells and three primary types of soluble or insoluble protein fibers: collagen fibers (tensile strength), reticular fibers (structural scaffolding), and elastic fibers (reversible compliance).

Based on density, cell type, and biochemical composition of matrix and fibers, connective tissue differentiates into:

  1. Connective tissue proper (loose or dense);
  2. Cartilaginous tissue: solid yet flexible gelled matrix;
  3. Adipose tissue: lipid-specialized cells;
  4. Bone tissue: mineralized extracellular matrix.
en.connective_adipose_nervous_section:
SPECIALIZED TISSUES: ADIPOSE AND NERVOUS SYSTEM

In summary: Among specialized connective tissues, adipose tissue governs energy and thermal homeostasis in its white and brown forms. The nervous tissue instead constitutes the body's integrated communication network: it leverages the bioelectricity of neurons and glial elements to convert physiological stimuli into chemical-electrical signals propagated unidirectionally at synapses.

TROPHOMECHANICAL FUNCTIONALITY AND ADIPOSE TISSUE (WHITE AND BROWN)

Connective tissue ensures metabolic cohesion and mechanical support to the body, mediating trophic exchanges for avascular tissues and guaranteeing an active immunological defense barrier through resident and migratory leukocyte populations.

A highly specialized form of connective tissue is ADIPOSE TISSUE, made up of endocrine and metabolic cells called adipocytes, whose primary function is the accumulation of lipids (mainly triglycerides) in the form of cytoplasmic lipid droplets. It is divided into two distinct structural and functional types:

  • White Adipose Tissue (Unilocular): Characterized by a single large lipid droplet that confines the nucleus and cytoplasm to the cellular periphery. It functions as the primary energy reserve, mechanical thermal insulator, and systemic endocrine organ (secretion of adipokines such as leptin).
  • Brown Adipose Tissue (Multilocular): Composed of cells rich in multiple lipid droplets and a high number of mitochondria. It is specialized in non-shivering thermogenesis: it dissipates the mitochondrial proton gradient producing thermal energy (heat) thanks to the specific expression of the channel protein UCP-1 (Thermogenin).

ORGANIZATION OF NERVOUS TISSUE AND ADULT NEUROGENESIS

Nervous tissue represents a highly integrated network dedicated to the reception, processing, and transmission of bioelectrical information. It consists of two fundamental cell populations: excitable cells (neurons) and neuroglia (glial cells), the latter essential for trophic and structural support, myelination, and homeostatic protection of neurons.

The primary functional unit is the neuron, anatomically structured into the following domains:

  • Soma (or Perikaryon): The cell body containing the nucleus and main metabolic organelles.
  • Dendrites: Branched afferent extensions dedicated to receiving nerve impulses coming from other neurons or the environment.
  • Axon: A single efferent extension, generally covered by an insulating myelin sheath, responsible for the rapid conduction of the action potential towards peripheral or central targets. Bundles of axons organized with covering connective tissues constitute peripheral nerves.

Highly differentiated neurons are traditionally considered perennial elements, stably locked in the G0 phase of the cell cycle. However, modern neurobiology has confirmed the presence of adult neurogenesis processes, driven by neural stem cells residing in specific microenvironmental brain niches (such as the subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus).

BIOELECTRIC PROPERTIES AND SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION

The propagation of the nerve impulse is based on two fundamental biophysical properties of the neuronal membrane:

  • Excitability: The ability to rapidly vary the resting membrane electrical potential in response to chemical-physical stimuli, converting them into an action potential.
  • Conductivity: The ability to actively and self-regeneratively propagate the action potential along the entire length of the axonal membrane without loss of amplitude.

Unidirectional communication between distinct neurons or between neurons and effector cells (muscle or gland cells) occurs at specialized functional junctions called SYNAPSES.

In chemical synapses, depolarization brought by the action potential to the presynaptic terminal triggers the influx of Ca2+ and the consequent exocytosis of neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft. Sequential binding of these signal molecules to specific receptors on the postsynaptic membrane generates graded potentials (excitatory or inhibitory), finely coordinating the neural network and the systemic integration of the organism.
